logline: A young ex-convict rebuilds his life and pursues revenge against a food-industry chaebol family by opening a bar-restaurant in Itaewon.

renewal.note: Completed 16-episode run in March 2020. Based on a completed webtoon; no sequel in development.

bollymeter.basis: Strong first half and a standout female lead offset by a mid-series tonal sprawl; audience scores sit notably higher than critical consensus.

seasons.review_body: Itaewon Class built its reputation on a revenge premise that feels grounded in labour economics and a chaebol critique rather than melodrama. The series ranks among the ten best Korean dramas on Netflix. Forbes named it one of the best K-dramas of 2020. The MyDramaList community settles at 8.4 across 99,000 users. The reception is more split: the social themes, the representation of queer and foreign characters, and Kim Da-mi's performance as a data-driven manager stand out, while a dissenting thread points to the second half, where the show tries to juggle too many thematic arcs at once, and where the revenge resolution lands more anticlimactically. The gap between cautious criticism and strong audience enthusiasm becomes the defining signal.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body: Itaewon Class Episode 1 aired January 31, 2020 on JTBC and delivered one of the most efficiently compressed premieres in K-drama: a father and son arriving in Itaewon, a single accident, and a decade of consequences established within a single episode. The premiere compresses tragedy without melodrama, establishing Park Saeroyi's motivation as moral rather than emotional - a decision that sets the show apart from the standard revenge K-drama register. Forbes would name it one of the best K-dramas of 2020, and the MyDramaList audience gave it 8.4 across 99,000 users. The South China Morning Post identified 'a mix of flawed but likeable characters, inspirational speeches on chasing dreams, and a love triangle that genuinely could go either way' - all of which are planted in the premiere.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A father and son arrive in Itaewon with exactly one year of freedom, and the episode ends with both gone - one dead, one imprisoned. The premiere compresses tragedy without melodrama, establishing Park Saeroyi's motivation as moral rather than emotional, which sets the show apart from standard revenge K-drama.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The accident and its immediate aftermath - ten minutes that make the following sixteen episodes feel inevitable.

critic_note.text: A mix of flawed but likeable characters, inspirational speeches on chasing dreams, and a love triangle that genuinely could go either way.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 2
episode_reviews.review_body: Itaewon Class Episode 2 aired February 1, 2020 on JTBC and introduced Jo Yi-seo - the data-driven social-media influencer whose entry into the show immediately reframes what the revenge arc might look like. Kim Da-mi's performance signals from her first scene that Yi-seo is the show's most unpredictable element: the extended look she gives Saeroyi when she walks into the bar tells the audience everything about who she is before she speaks. The episode's parallel work - establishing Saeroyi's bar-opening conviction alongside Yi-seo's cold assessment of its commercial prospects - is the clearest early evidence that the show's thematic interests are broader than personal revenge.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Prison and release, and then: Itaewon. Saeroyi opens his bar with nothing except conviction, and Jo Yi-seo enters the story with a social-media presence that immediately reframes what the revenge arc might look like. Kim Da-mi's performance signals early that she is the show's most unpredictable element.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Yi-seo walking into the bar and assessing it, then Saeroyi, in a single extended look that tells the audience everything about who she is.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 9
episode_reviews.review_body: Itaewon Class Episode 9 aired February 28, 2020 on JTBC and is the episode critics and audience reviewers most frequently identify as the show's tonal high-water mark. The Danbam team achieves real momentum as a going concern, and the show's themes around race, queerness, and class are most elegantly integrated before the back half begins adding antagonist threads that stretch the structure. The MyDramaList community's observation that the show's second half 'tries to juggle too many thematic arcs at once' points to the midpoint as the optimum of the series' coherence - Episode 9 is the episode where the show was doing exactly what Forbes and the MyDramaList 8.4 audience rating suggest it could do.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The bar achieves its first real momentum and the show's themes around race, queerness, and class are most elegantly integrated here before the back half starts adding antagonist threads. The episode is the high-water mark of the show's tonal coherence.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Danbam team's first night feeling like a going concern - small but earned after nine episodes of grinding.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 16
episode_reviews.review_body: Itaewon Class Episode 16 aired March 21, 2020 on JTBC as the series finale, drawing 16.548 percent peak nationwide ratings. The finale resolves the corporate revenge arc with more pragmatism than catharsis - a deliberate choice that divided audiences who had been anticipating a cleaner victory against the Jangga chairman. The love-triangle resolution lands more satisfyingly than the business plot, with Yi-seo's arc reaching a conclusion that honours the complexity Kim Da-mi had built across sixteen episodes. Saeroyi's final conversation with the chairman is the episode's most debated scene - the show choosing complexity over the clean win its audience had been running on emotional credit to receive.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale resolves the corporate revenge arc with more pragmatism than catharsis, which divided audiences expecting a cleaner victory. The love-triangle resolution is more satisfying than the business plot. The closing image is of a man who got what he wanted and is ambivalently at peace with it.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Saeroyi's final conversation with the Jangga chairman - the show choosing complexity over the clean win its audience had been anticipating.
